en: Parivāra 4.
Antarapeyyāla: Section on Questions on a Few Items (Katipucchāvāra)
How many offenses are there?
How many classes of offenses are there?
How many bases for training are there?
How many kinds of disrespect are there?
How many kinds of respect are there?
How many bases for training are there?
How many failures are there?
How many origins of offenses are there?
How many roots of dispute are there?
How many roots of censure are there?
How many qualities conducive to cordiality are there?
How many grounds for schism are there?
How many legal issues?
How many means of settling?
Five offenses.
The five classes of offenses.
The five bases for training.
The seven offenses.
The seven classes of offenses.
The seven grounds for disciplinary action.
The six kinds of disrespect.
The six respects.
The six grounds for discipline.
The four failures.
There are six origins of offenses,
six roots of disputes,
and six roots of accusations.
The six principles of conciliation;
the eighteen grounds for schism;
the four types of legal issues.
Seven grounds for reconciliation.
In this context, what are the five kinds of offenses?

An offense involving defeat (pārājika), an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), an offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), an offense requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
These are the five kinds of offenses.
In this regard, what are the five classes of offenses?

The class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya), the class of offenses requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), and the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
These are the five classes of offenses.
In this regard, what are the five bases for training?

Refraining from, abstaining from, desisting from, avoiding, not doing, not performing, not committing, not transgressing the limit, and destroying the bridge with respect to these five classes of offenses.
These are the five bases for training.
In this regard, what are the seven offenses?

An offense entailing defeat (pārājika), an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), an offense of grave transgression (thullaccaya), an offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita).
These are the seven offenses.
In this regard, what are the seven classes of offenses?

The class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of grave offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring confession (pācittiya), the class of offenses to be acknowledged (pāṭidesanīya), the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and the class of offenses of improper speech (dubbhāsita).
These are the seven classes of offenses.
In this regard, what are the seven bases for training?

Refraining from, abstaining from, desisting from, avoiding, non-doing, non-committing, non-transgression, not overstepping the limit, and destroying the bridge [of transgression] with respect to these seven classes of offenses—[this is the seventh basis for training].
These are the seven grounds for training.
In this regard, what are the six kinds of disrespect?

Disrespect toward the Buddha, disrespect toward the Dhamma, disrespect toward the Saṅgha, disrespect toward the training, disrespect toward heedfulness, and disrespect toward the distribution of requisites.
These are the six kinds of disrespect.
In that regard, what are the six kinds of respect?
Respect for the Buddha, respect for the Dhamma, respect for the Saṅgha, respect for the training, respect for heedfulness, and respect for frugality.
These are the six respects.
In this context, what are the six bases for training?
Refraining from, abstaining from, desisting from, avoiding, not doing, not committing, not transgressing, not overstepping the limit, and destroying the bridge of the six types of disrespect.
These are the six grounds for training.
In this regard, what are the four failures?
Failure in virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view, and failure in livelihood.
These are the four failures.
In this regard, what are the six origins of offenses?
There is an offense that originates from the body, but not from speech or mind.
There is an offense that originates from speech, not from body or mind;
there is an offense that originates from both body and speech, not from mind;
there is an offense that originates from both body and mind, not from speech.
There is an offense that originates from speech and mind, but not from body;
there is an offense that originates from body, speech, and mind—
these are the six origins of offenses.
In this regard, what are the six roots of dispute?
Here, a monk is prone to anger and resentment.
That monk who is prone to anger and resentment dwells without respect and without deference even toward the Teacher, and likewise toward the Dhamma...
He dwells without respect and without deference; he dwells without respect and without deference toward the Saṅgha as well, and he does not fulfill the training.
That bhikkhu who dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher, [toward] the Dhamma …pe… toward the Saṅgha …pe…
One who does not fulfill the training creates a dispute within the Saṅgha.
Such a dispute is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including both devas and humans.
If you should perceive such a root of dispute either within yourselves or externally, you should strive there for the abandoning of that very evil root of dispute.
If you do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, you should practice for the sake of ensuring that this evil root of dispute does not flow forth in the future.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute;
in this way, there is the non-outflow of this evil root of dispute in the future.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who slanders and is spiteful ... [as before] ...
he is envious and miserly, fraudulent and deceitful, has evil desires and wrong view, and is one who clings to his own views, holding them dogmatically and being difficult to disabuse of them.
That monk who clings to his own views, holds them dogmatically, and is difficult to disabuse of them, is disrespectful even toward the Teacher.
He dwells without deference; he dwells disrespectful and undeferential even toward the Dhamma; he dwells disrespectful and undeferential even toward the Saṅgha;
he does not fulfill the training.
That monk who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, [and similarly] toward the Dhamma... [and so on].
In the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ... he does not fulfill the training; he creates a dispute in the Saṅgha.
That dispute leads to the harm of many people, to the unhappiness of many people, to the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including both devas and humans.
If you perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, you should strive there for the abandonment of that very evil root of dispute.
If you do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, you should practice there for the sake of its non-recurrence in the future.
In this way, there is the abandonment of that evil root of dispute.
In this way, there is no further influx of this evil root of dispute.
These are the six roots of dispute.
In that regard, what are the six roots of reproach?
In this case, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and resentment.
That bhikkhu who is prone to anger and resentment dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher;
he dwells without respect and without deference toward the Dhamma; he dwells without respect and without deference toward the Saṅgha; and he does not fulfill the training.
That monk who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma, ...
toward the Saṅgha, ...
and who does not fulfill the training, creates censure within the Saṅgha.
Whatever reproach there may be that is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including both devas and humans—
if you should perceive such a root of reproach within yourselves or externally, you should strive for the abandonment of that very evil root of reproach.
If you do not perceive such a root of reproach, either internally or externally, then you should practice for the sake of preventing the future outflow of that very same evil root of reproach.
In this way, there is the abandoning of that evil root of reproach;
in this way, there is the non-outflow of that evil root of reproach in the future.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu is one who slanders and is spiteful...
he is envious and miserly; he is fraudulent and deceitful; he has evil desires and wrong view; he is one who clings to his own views, holding them firmly and being difficult to disabuse of them.
That bhikkhu who clings to his own views, holding them firmly and being difficult to disabuse of them, is disrespectful even toward the Teacher.
He dwells without deference; he dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Dhamma as well, and he dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Saṅgha as well;
he does not fulfill the training.
That monk who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, [and] toward the Dhamma... [and so forth].
In the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ...one who does not fulfill the training creates censure within the Saṅgha.
Such censure is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.
If you perceive such a root of reproach within yourself or externally, you should strive for the abandonment of that very evil root of reproach.
If you do not perceive such a root of reproach within yourself or externally, you should practice so that that very evil root of reproach does not flow forth in the future.
In this way, there is the abandonment of that evil root of reproach.
In this way, there is no further outflow of this root of reproach that is evil.
These are the six roots of reproach.
In this regard, what are the six principles of cordiality?
Here, a bhikkhu maintains loving-kindness in bodily action toward his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private.
This quality is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu maintains loving-kindness in verbal action toward his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, a monk maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, whatever gains are righteous and righteously obtained—even if only the mere contents of his alms-bowl—a monk shares such gains with his virtuous companions in the holy life, not hoarding them for himself.
This quality is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, those precepts which are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, untainted, liberating...
He dwells having attained a commonality of virtue with his fellow celibates—virtue that is praised by the wise, unadulterated, and conducive to concentration—in both public and private.
This quality, too, is consoling, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, whatever view is noble, leading out, and leads its practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering—a monk dwells in conformity with such a view together with his fellow celibates, both openly and in private.
This too is a principle of courtesy that creates affection, creates respect, and leads to gathering together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
These are the six principles of courtesy.
In this regard, what are the eighteen grounds for schism?
Here, a monk proclaims what is non-Dhamma as "Dhamma," proclaims Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," proclaims what is non-Vinaya as "Vinaya," and proclaims Vinaya as "non-Vinaya";
he proclaims what was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as "spoken and uttered [by him]."
He proclaims that which was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken, not uttered by the Tathāgata";
he proclaims that which was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata"; he proclaims that which was practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata";
and he proclaims that which was not laid down by the Tathāgata as "laid down by the Tathāgata."
He represents what has been laid down by the Tathāgata as "not laid down by the Tathāgata"; he represents an offense as "no offense";
he represents no offense as "an offense"; he represents a light offense as "a heavy offense";
he represents a heavy offense as "a light offense"; he represents an offense with remainder as "an offense without remainder."
He proclaims a non-residual offense as a "residual offense"; he proclaims a grave offense as "not grave";
he proclaims a non-grave offense as "grave.
These are the eighteen grounds for schism.
In this context, what are the four legal issues?
The legal issue of dispute, the legal issue of accusation, the legal issue of offense, and the legal issue of business—
these are the four legal issues.
In this regard, what are the seven principles for settling disputes?

Resolution face-to-face, resolution through recollection, resolution because of past insanity, acting according to what has been admitted, majority decision, further penalty, and covering over as with grass—
these are the seven principles for settling disputes.
The Section on Questions has been concluded.
Its summary verse is:
Offense, categories of offenses,
Furthermore, the disciplined are sevenfold: the disciplined,
those lacking respect, those possessing respect, and the root itself.
Furthermore: the defeats,
the origins, the disputes,
the accusations, and the matter to be remembered.
And by means of the section on differentiation; thus,
existence itself is stated as the settling [factors],
and these are the seventeen terms.
4.1. Chapter on the Origination of Offenses by Six (Cha-āpatti-samuṭṭhāna-vāra).
Could one incur a *pārājika* offense through the first origination of an offense?
It should be said: "No."
Would he commit a *saṅghādisesa* offense?
It should be said: "He might.
Would he commit a grave offense (*thullaccaya*)?
It may be said: "It could be. Would one incur a pācittiya offense? It may be said: "It could be."
Would one incur an offense entailing confession?
It should be said: "It may. Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing? It should be said: "It may."
"It should be said: 'It might be.
"Would he incur a wrong speech?
"It should be said: 'No.'"
Could one incur a *pārājika* offense by means of the second origin of offenses?
One should say: "No.
Could one incur a *saṅghādisesa* offense [by that same means]?
It may be said: "It could be so.
Would he incur a grave offense (thullaccaya)?
It may be said: "It could be so."
"Would one incur a pācittiya offense? "It may be," it should be said.
"Would one incur a pāṭidesanīya offense?"
"It should be said: 'No.
Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)? It should be said: 'It may.'"
"Would one incur a grave offense (dubbhāsita)?
"One should say: 'No.
"Would one incur a defeat (pārājika) by means of the third origin of offenses?"
"It should not be said [that he does not].
Should he incur a *saṅghādisesa* offense?
"It may be so," it should be said.
"Would one incur a thullaccaya offense?
"It may be so," it should be said. "Would one incur a pācittiya offense?"
It may be said: "It could be.
Could one incur an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*)?
It may be said: "It could be."
Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)?
It should be said: "It might. Would one incur an offense of ill-spokenness (dubbhāsita)? It should be said: "It might."
"It should not be said [that it does not happen].
"Could one incur a *pārājika* offense through the fourth origin of offenses?
"It could," it should be said.
"Would he incur a saṅghādisesa offense?
"It may be so," one should say.
"Would he incur a thullaccaya offense?"
It may be said: "Yes. Would one incur a pācittiya offense?
It may be said: "Yes."
Would one incur an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya)?
It should be said: “It may. Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)? It should be said: “It may.”
It should be said: "Yes.
Would he incur an offense of wrong speech?
It should be said: "No."
Could one incur a *pārājika* offense by means of the fifth origin of offenses?
It should be said: "It could. Could one incur a *saṅghādisesa* offense [by that same means]?
"It may be so," it should be said.
"Would he incur a grave offense (thullaccaya)?
"It may be so," it should be said.
"Would he incur a pācittiya offense?
"It may be so," one should say.
"Would he incur a pāṭidesanīya offense?"
"It should be said: 'No.
Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)? It should be said: 'It may.'"
"Could one incur a grave offense of wrong speech? "It could be so," it should be said.
"Could one incur a *pārājika* offense by means of the sixth origin of offenses?"
It may be so; it should be said "it may be. Would he incur a *saṅghādisesa* offense? It may be so; it should be said "it may be."
"Would he incur a thullaccaya offense?
"It should be said: 'He might.
"Would he incur a pācittiya offense?"
It may be said: "It could be.
Could one incur an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*)?
It may be said: "It could be."
Would one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)?
It should be said: "It may. Would one incur an offense of ill-spokenness (dubbhāsita)? It should be said: "It may."
"No, it should not be said so.
The first section, the Chapter on the Origination of the Six Offenses, is finished.
4.2. The Chapter on Committed Offenses.
How many offenses does one commit through the first origin of offenses?
Through the first origin of offenses, one commits five offenses.

When a bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, has a hut built by means of solicitation, on ground not already prepared for construction, exceeding the proper measure, involving destruction, and lacking space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of undertaking.
If even a single morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that morsel arrives, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
If a monk, perceiving it as allowable, eats food at an improper time, there is an offense of pācittiya.

If a monk, perceiving it as permissible, receives fresh or cooked food directly from the hand of an unrelated nun who has entered an inhabited area and eats it, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
Through this first origin of offenses, he incurs these five offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they included?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
Among the four types of legal issues, which type of legal issue is it?
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are included within five classes of offenses:

they may be included within the class of offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*), the class of grave offenses (*thullaccaya*), the class of offenses entailing expiation (*pācittiya*), the class of offenses entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*), or the class of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from the body, not from speech, nor from the mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue of an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles for settling.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
How many offenses does one commit through the second origin of offenses?
Through the second origin of offenses, one commits four offenses:

A bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, gives instructions: “Build a hut for me. They build his hut on a site that has not been declared allowable, which exceeds the proper measurements, involves injury to living beings, and lacks space on all sides. For the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when one bundle of materials has not yet arrived, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
when that bundle has arrived, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, recites the Dhamma word by word to one who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By means of this second origin of offenses, he incurs these four offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are included within four classes of offenses:

they may be included within the class of offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), they may be included within the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), they may be included within the class of offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya), or they may be included within the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from speech, not from body or mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
Regarding the third origin of offenses, how many offenses does one incur?
Regarding the third origin of offenses, one incurs five offenses.

If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, having made an arrangement, builds a hut on a site not formally authorized, exceeding the proper dimensions, involving destruction, and lacking space on all sides: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of undertaking;
when one bundle of materials has not yet arrived, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*);
when that bundle has arrived, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, requests exquisite foods for his own sake and eats them, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, eats without restraining a bhikkhunī who is giving directions [to a donor], he commits an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya).
By means of this third origin of offenses, one incurs these five offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? ...
To how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures.
It may be a failure in virtue; it may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, it is comprised within five classes of offenses:

it may be an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), it may be a grave offense (thullaccaya), it may be an offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), it may be an offense requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), or it may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from both body and speech, but not from mind.
Of the four legal issues, it is the legal issue of an offense.
Of the seven methods for settling disputes, by how many methods are they settled?

They may be settled by both *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been admitted); or they may be settled by both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass).
Regarding the fourth origin of offenses, how many offenses does one incur?
By means of the fourth origin of offenses, one incurs six offenses:
if a bhikkhu engages in sexual intercourse, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);

if a bhikkhu, perceiving it as improper, builds a hut by his own request, where the site has not been approved, which exceeds the proper dimensions, involves destruction, and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of undertaking.
If even a single morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that morsel has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as improper, eats food at an improper time, there is an offense of pācittiya.

If a monk, perceiving it as improper, receives with his own hand solid or soft food from an unrelated nun who has entered an inhabited area and eats it, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
He incurs these six offenses through the fourth origin of offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses pertain to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
The seven classes of offenses are comprised within six classes of offenses: they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika),
the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring confession (pācittiya),
the class of offenses requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), or the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from both body and mind, but not from speech.
Of the four legal issues, it is the legal issue of an offense.
Of the seven methods of settling disputes, by how many methods are they settled?

They may be settled by both *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what is admitted); or they may be settled by both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass).
Regarding the fifth origin of offenses, how many offenses does one incur?
By means of the fifth origin of offenses, one incurs six offenses.
A bhikkhu who is of evil desires and overcome by longing utters a non-existent, unreal claim to a superhuman state: an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).

A bhikkhu, perceiving it as improper, gives instructions: “Build a hut for me. They build his hut on a site that has not been pointed out, which exceeds the proper measure, involves destruction of vegetation, and lacks a space on all sides. For the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When one verse-quarter has been reached, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that verse-quarter has been completed, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If a monk, perceiving it as improper, recites the Dhamma word-by-word to one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of pācittiya.

If, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate, one speaks what is low by way of what is low out of a desire for sport, there is an offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*).
By means of this fifth origin of offenses, one incurs these six offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
The seven classes of offenses are subsumed under six classes of offenses: they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika),
the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya),
the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), or the class of offenses of improper speech (dubbhāsita).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from both speech and mind, not from body.
Of the four types of legal issues, it is the legal issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven methods for settling disputes, by how many methods are they settled?
They may be settled by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; or they may be settled by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
By means of the sixth origin of offenses, how many offenses does one incur?
Through the sixth origin of offenses, one incurs six offenses:
if a monk, having made an agreement, steals goods, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);

if a monk, perceiving something as improper, having made an agreement, builds a hut on a site that has not been approved, which exceeds the proper measure, involves destruction of life, and lacks a space around it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of undertaking.
If even a single morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that morsel arrives, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
If a bhikkhu, perceiving it as improper, requests fine foods for his own sake and eats them, there is an offense of pācittiya.
If a monk, perceiving it as improper, eats without having restrained a nun who is giving directions, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
By means of this sixth origin of offenses, he incurs these six offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
Among the four kinds of legal issues, to which legal issue do they belong?
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
The seven classes of offenses are comprised within six classes of offenses: they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika),
the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring confession (pācittiya),
the class of offenses requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), or the class of wrong-doings (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four legal issues, it is the legal issue of an offense.
Of the seven methods for settling disputes, they are settled by three methods:
sometimes by face-to-face resolution and by acting according to what is admitted; sometimes by face-to-face resolution and by covering over as with grass.
The second section, concerning the origin of offenses among the six origins of offenses, is finished.
4.3. Verses on the Origins of Offenses The origins [of offenses] pertaining to the body have been declared by the One of Infinite Vision,
the Benefactor of the World, who perceives solitude.
"How many offenses have arisen from that?
I ask you, O expert in the Vibhaṅga, tell me.
What are the bodily origins [of these offenses], O Seer of the Infinite?"
They were proclaimed by the one who seeks the world's welfare and perceives seclusion;
five offenses have arisen from him.
This I declare to you, O you who are skilled in the analysis [of the Vinaya].
The verbal origins have been declared by the one of infinite vision,
the benefactor of the world who perceives solitude;
how many offenses have arisen from them?
I ask you, speak, O expert in the Vibhaṅga!
The verbal origins have been declared by the one of infinite vision,
the benefactor of the world who perceives seclusion.
Four offenses have arisen from that;
this I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅga.
Their origins are physical and verbal, according to the one of infinite vision.
They have been proclaimed by the one who benefits the world and perceives seclusion;
how many offenses have arisen from them?
I ask you; speak, O expert in the Vibhaṅga.
The origins of bodily and verbal [actions] have been declared by the one of infinite vision,
the benefactor of the world who perceives solitude;
five classes of offenses have arisen from them.
This I declare to you, O you who are skilled in analysis:
the bodily and mental origins have been explained by the one of infinite vision,
the benefactor of the world, who perceives solitude.
"How many offenses have arisen from that?
I ask you; tell me, O expert in the Vibhaṅga.
Are the origins bodily or mental, O Seer of the Infinite?"
They have been declared by the one who seeks the welfare of the world and perceives solitude;
six classes of offenses have arisen from him.
This I declare to you, O you who are skilled in the analysis [of the Vinaya].
The origins of offenses— verbal and mental— have been declared by the Seer of the Infinite,
the Benefactor of the World who perceives seclusion.
How many offenses have arisen from those origins?
I ask you, speak, O master skilled in analysis!
You who see the infinite, who look upon seclusion, and who work for the welfare of the world, you have explained the origins of verbal and mental actions.
Six offenses have arisen from that;
this I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅga.
Their origins—bodily, verbal, and mental—were seen by the One of Infinite Vision.
The one who seeks the welfare of the world and perceives seclusion has proclaimed them;
how many offenses have arisen from that?
I ask you, O expert in the Vibhaṅga—please tell me.
Origination is physical, verbal, and mental,
as taught by the All-Seeing One, the Benefactor of the World who perceives seclusion;
by him, six classes of offenses arising therefrom were declared.
"This I declare to you, O you who are skilled in analysis.
The third verse on the origins of offenses is concluded.
4.4. The Section on Failures and Conditions.
On account of a failure in virtue, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a failure in virtue, one incurs four offenses:
if a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals an offense entailing defeat, she incurs an offense entailing defeat.
If she conceals a matter of doubt, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
if a monk conceals a saṅghādisesa offense, there is an offense of pācittiya;
if he conceals his own grave offense (duṭṭhulla), there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
On account of failure in virtue, one incurs these four offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
…pe… By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within four classes of offenses.

It may be a class of offense involving defeat (pārājika), it may be a class of grave offense (thullaccaya), it may be a class of offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what is admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
On account of a failure in conduct, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a failure in conduct, one incurs one offense:
if one conceals a failure in conduct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
On account of failure in conduct, one incurs this one offense.
To how many of the four failures does that offense belong?
… [as before] … By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes is it settled?
That offense belongs to one of the four failures— namely,
failure in conduct—
and is included within one of the seven classes of offenses.
It belongs to the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
it may be settled by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; or it may be settled by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
On account of failure in view, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of failure in view, one incurs two offenses:
for not relinquishing an evil view after being pressed up to three times, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the formal motion (*ñatti*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*):
one incurs these two offenses on account of failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*).
To which of the four failures do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses belong to one of the four failures—
namely, failure in conduct.
They are included within two classes of offenses among the seven classes of offenses:
they may be included within the class of offenses of expiation (pācittiya), or they may be included within the class of offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
They originate from one of the six origins of offenses.
They originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
On account of failure in livelihood, how many offenses does one commit?
On account of failure in livelihood, one commits six offenses.

If, for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by desire falsely claims a non-existent, unactualized superhuman state, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If, for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one engages in matchmaking, it is an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa).

If, for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one says, "The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant," it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) for the person who understands [the meaning].
If a monk, for the sake of his livelihood and as a means of livelihood, requests fine foods for his own benefit and eats them, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
If a nun, for the sake of her livelihood and as a means of livelihood, requests fine foods for her own benefit and eats them, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya).
If one who is not ill, for the sake of their livelihood and as a means of livelihood, requests either soup or rice for their own benefit and eats it, they commit an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Due to failure in livelihood, one incurs these six offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? … [etc.
… By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, they are included within six classes of offenses.

It may be by way of the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), it may be by way of the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), it may be by way of the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya),
it may be by way of the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya), it may be by way of the class of offenses requiring confession (pāṭidesanīya),
or it may be by way of the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from six origins.
It may arise from the body, not from speech or mind;
it may arise from speech, not from body or mind;
it may arise from both body and speech, not from the mind.
There may be [kamma] that originates from both body and mind, but not from speech;
there may be [kamma] that originates from both speech and mind, but not from body;
and there may be [kamma] that originates from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what is admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
The fourth section on the conditions for failure is finished.
4.5. Section on the Conditions for Legal Issues:
On account of what legal issue does one incur how many offenses? On account of a legal issue arising from a dispute, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a legal issue arising from a dispute, one incurs two offenses:
if one reviles one who is fully ordained, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya);
if one reviles one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
On account of a legal issue arising from a dispute, one incurs these two offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
… [and so on] … by how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to one of the four failures—
namely, failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, they are included in two classes of offenses.
It may be a class of offenses involving an offense of expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of offenses involving an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from three origins:
they may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech.
They may originate from speech and mind, but not from body;
they may originate from body, speech, and mind.
Among the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), it is the issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
Of the seven methods of settling disputes, they are settled by three methods:
sometimes by face-to-face settlement and by acting according to what is admitted; sometimes by face-to-face settlement and by covering over as with grass.
On account of a legal issue arising from an accusation, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a legal issue arising from a formal accusation, one incurs three offenses:
if one groundlessly charges a bhikkhu with an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), it is an offense of formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa);
if one groundlessly charges him with an offense of formal meeting of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one accuses another of a groundless failure in conduct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
By reason of this legal issue arising from a formal accusation, one incurs these three offenses.
To which of the four failures do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within three classes of offenses:

they may be included in the class of offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*), they may be included in the class of offenses entailing expiation (*pācittiya*), or they may be included in the class of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from three origins:
There may be [kamma] that originates from both body and mind, but not from speech;
there may be [kamma] that originates from both speech and mind, but not from body;
and there may be [kamma] that originates from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
How many offenses does one commit as a result of a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*)?
One commits four offenses as a result of a legal issue arising from an offense.
If a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), she commits an offense entailing expulsion.
If she conceals a state of doubt, it is an offense of thullaccaya;
if a monk conceals a saṅghādisesa offense, it is an offense of pācittiya;
if he conceals a failure in conduct, it is an offense of dukkaṭa.
Due to the legal issue arising from an offense, one incurs these four offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong? … [etc.
… By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures—
sometimes they are a failure of virtue, sometimes they are a failure of conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, they are included within four classes of offenses.

It may be a class of offense involving defeat (pārājika), it may be a class of grave offense (thullaccaya), it may be a class of offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
On account of what kind of legal issue (adhikaraṇa) does one incur how many offenses?
On account of a legal issue arising from business (kicca), one incurs five offenses.

When a nun who follows one who has been suspended (ukkhitānuvattikā) does not desist even after being pressed up to the third time, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the formal motion (ñatti).
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
For monks who follow those who cause a schism, if they do not desist after being admonished up to three times, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If one does not relinquish a wrong view after being admonished up to three times, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
On account of this legal issue arising from a formal act (kiccādhikaraṇa), one incurs these five offenses.
To which of the four failures (vipatti) do those offenses belong? …pe…
By how many of the seven methods of settlement are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within five classes of offenses:

they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya), or the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
Excluding the seven offenses and the seven classes of offenses, to how many of the four failures (*vipatti*) do the remaining offenses belong?
And by how many of the seven classes of offenses are they subsumed?
From how many origins do the six origins of offenses arise?
To which of the four legal issues (adhikaraṇa) do they belong?
By how many means of settlement (samatha) among the seven are they settled?
Excluding the seven classes of offenses and the seven groups of offenses, to which of the four failures do the remaining offenses belong?
By which of the seven groups of offenses are they included?
By which of the six origins of offenses do they originate?
Of the four kinds of legal issues, which one is it?
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, by which principle are they settled?
For what reason?
"Except for the seven offenses and the seven classes of offenses, there are no other offenses.
The fifth section on the conditions for legal issues is finished.
The intermediate series is finished.
Its summary verse:
The questions asked, the origins,
and likewise the offenses committed.
Origin, failure,
and likewise through legal issues.
